directions: Give Windamere Palm a warm, sheltered site with deep, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil, since this Himalayan foothill native prefers more consistent moisture and humidity than the common windmill palm. It is markedly less cold-hardy than Trachycarpus fortunei, reliably surviving only into the upper teens to low 20s Fahrenheit, so it suits protected zone 9-11 gardens rather than colder zone 8 sites. The thick, closely ringed trunk and unusually broad, stiff leaf segments make it a striking specimen for collectors once it clears seedling stage, though growth is slow for the first several years. Shelter young plants from harsh drying wind and hard freezes with frost cloth until well established.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

directions: Plant Yunnan Dwarf Windmill Palm in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, mimicking the high-elevation Chinese mountain forests where it grows as groundcover beneath taller trees. Unlike its tree-forming relatives, this species keeps its trunk entirely underground, sending up only a low, dense clump of stiff, often blue-tinted fan leaves rarely exceeding a few feet in height and spread. Its subterranean growing point makes it exceptionally cold-hardy for a fan palm, tolerating winters into the low single digits Fahrenheit once established, making it one of the hardiest true palms available for zone 7 gardens. Water regularly the first year or two, then reduce to occasional deep watering during dry spells.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

common_name: Himalayan Windmill Palm (Khasia Hills Fan Palm)
directions: Grow Himalayan Windmill Palm in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade on a warm, sheltered site, since it comes from steep montane cliffs and forest edges of Nepal, northeast India, and northern Myanmar and prefers more warmth than the common windmill palm. It tolerates brief cold into the mid-to-upper teens Fahrenheit once well established but is noticeably more cold-sensitive than Trachycarpus fortunei, making it best suited to zone 9-11 gardens rather than colder zone 8 sites. The slender gray trunk carries dark green fan leaves with a distinctive bluish-gray reverse, giving mature specimens an elegant, two-toned crown. Protect young palms from hard freezes and drying winter wind until the trunk has developed some height.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

common_name: Mexican Dwarf Blue Palm (Sierra Madre Palm)
directions: Plant Mexican Dwarf Blue Palm in lean, rocky or gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, matching the limestone hillsides of Nuevo Leon, Mexico where it grows naturally. Its low, clustering, decumbent trunks creep along or just beneath the soil surface rather than standing upright, forming a wide clump of stiff, silvery-blue fan leaves that rarely exceeds about 6 feet tall but can spread considerably wider over time. This is one of the more cold-hardy Brahea species, tolerating brief dips into the mid-to-upper teens Fahrenheit once established, and it is highly drought-tolerant, failing quickly in soggy or heavy clay soil. Use it as a striking small-scale accent or rock-garden specimen in zone 8-11 xeriscape and dry-garden plantings.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

common_name: Dwarf Rock Palm (Sierra Madre Oriental Palm)
directions: Grow Dwarf Rock Palm in lean, fast-draining, rocky soil in partial shade, echoing the dry, high-elevation oak forests of northeastern Mexico's Sierra Madre Oriental where it grows as an understory palm. It is the smallest species in its genus, forming a trunkless rosette of dark green fan leaves with striking silvery-white undersides, rarely reaching more than 4 feet tall or wide even after many years. Despite its diminutive size and mountain-forest origin, it is surprisingly cold-hardy, tolerating brief freezes down to around 14 degrees F once established, making it a choice miniature specimen for shaded rock gardens in zone 8-11. Keep it on the dry side, especially in winter, since it is intolerant of poorly drained or waterlogged soil.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

directions: Plant San Jose Hesper Palm in well-drained soil in full sun; it is native to canyon slopes in the southern Baja California peninsula and mainland Sonora and Sinaloa, and unlike most of its Brahea relatives it tolerates the humidity of Gulf Coast and Florida gardens quite well rather than demanding bone-dry conditions. It is a slow-growing, solitary, blue-gray-leaved fan palm that develops a tall, slender trunk over many decades, reliably taking cold to about 25 degrees F and briefly surviving dips into the upper teens once well established. Water regularly while young to speed establishment, then reduce to occasional deep watering, as mature specimens are quite drought-tolerant.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

directions: Plant Carnarvon Fan Palm in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; native to sandstone gorges of central Queensland, Australia, it is the fastest-growing member of its genus in cultivation, reaching landscape size in a fraction of the time required by the related Chinese Fan Palm or Australian Cabbage Palm. It develops a tall, ringed trunk topped by a full crown of glossy, deep green fan leaves and is regarded as the most cold-hardy Livistona species commonly grown, tolerating brief freezes down to around 24 degrees F once established. Water regularly during establishment and dry spells; a fast-growing, low-maintenance choice for zone 9-11 landscapes wanting a mature palm silhouette sooner than most fan palms provide.

common_name: Red Cabbage Palm (Central Australian Cabbage Palm)
directions: Plant Red Cabbage Palm in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; it is native to a single isolated oasis population at Palm Valley in Australia's arid Northern Territory, where its roots reach permanent underground water despite scorching desert heat above ground. New leaves emerge with a striking reddish-bronze flush before maturing to green, giving the species its common name, and it develops a tall, solitary, ringed trunk over time. It handles heat and drought remarkably well once its roots are established and has proven surprisingly cold-tolerant for a desert-oasis palm, briefly surviving temperatures near 23 degrees F, but it is best reserved for zone 9-11 gardens where the trunk is not stressed by prolonged hard freezes. Provide supplemental water during extended dry spells to keep growth steady.

Plant this naturally occurring hybrid between California Fan Palm (Washingtonia filifera) and Mexican Fan Palm (W. robusta) in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. It combines the faster growth and taller, more elegant silhouette of W. robusta with the greater cold tolerance and stockier trunk of W. filifera, making it noticeably hardier than pure W. robusta and able to shrug off freezes into the mid-teens Fahrenheit once well established, with foliage regrowing after occasional harder freeze damage. Seedlings show intermediate, variable characteristics since this is a hybrid rather than a fixed species, so expect some variation in trunk thickness and growth rate between individual plants. Drought-tolerant once established and well suited to zone 8-11 gardens seeking a large, fast fan palm with extra cold insurance over Mexican Fan Palm alone.
